```sh
podnet warp forward --list          # the forwards of the detached instances
podnet warp run -- curl https://cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace
podnet warp tun --interface podnet0        # TUN interface (needs CAP_NET_ADMIN)
podnet warp up                      # a proxy in the background for this sandbox
eval "$(podnet warp env)"           # a shell joins it
podnet warp exec -- git clone ...   # a program under the pod of the proxy
podnet warp nc HOST PORT            # a byte pipe, for an SSH ProxyCommand
podnet warp down                    # stop it
```

## Device and state

* The device and its key are in `warp.json` in the state directory: the
  first that podnet can write of `PODNET_STATE_DIR`, `$XDG_STATE_HOME/podnet`,
  `~/.local/state/podnet`, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podnet` and `podnet-<uid>` in the
  temporary directory. The file mode is 0600. podnet checks the directory
  before it registers a device. podnet writes no file in a directory of
  another user (root with the `HOME` of a user): the state directory skips
  that `HOME`, and `warp ssh-config --write`, `warp up --persist` and
  `--env-d`, and `autostart` exit 78. `PODNET_FOREIGN_HOME=allow` writes
  anyway. Use `--identity PATH` for a different file,
  `--ephemeral` or `PODNET_STATE_DIR=none` to use a new device for one run.
* IPv6: the stack has the IPv4 and the IPv6 address of the device. The
  proxy asks for A and AAAA records through the tunnel and tries IPv4
  first, then IPv6, so a host with only AAAA records works too.
  `warp tun` adds the IPv6 address (/128) to the interface.
* What a destination sees (measured by a tester on 0.3.0-beta.8; issue
  183): not the address of the device (`172.16.0.2`, `2606:4700:110:...`),
  but an egress address of Cloudflare. The egress address stays the same
  in one MASQUE session, and a new session gets a new one (IPv6 from a
  `2a09:bac1::/32` or `2a09:bac5::/32` prefix). The `--listen` listeners of
  one proxy share one session and one address; each `--listen-identity`
  has its own device, session and address. `warp rotate` changes the
  MASQUE key only. `cdn-cgi/trace` gives the IPv4 `ip=` also for an IPv6
  flow.
* `--session-max-age SECS` (or `PODNET_WARP_SESSION_MAX_AGE`) closes each
  session at that age and opens a new one, with a new egress address, for
  `warp proxy`, `forward`, `run`, `up` and `tun`. The TCP flows of the old
  session end. Default: off. The log gives the cause of each close of a
  session.
* `--probe IP:PORT` (default `1.1.1.1:443`) is the TCP probe of the data
  path. A session can carry ICMP and UDP but no TCP. Each 30 s podnet
  connects to the target through the session (`warp tun`: one SYN from the
  tunnel address and port 61999; the answer does not go to the TUN). After
  3 failures in a row, a new session takes the new flows (the log names
  `reason=tcp-probe`). `--probe off` stops it.
* New devices: the WARP service limits the registrations of each address.
  Observed: HTTP 429 (error 1015) after about 10 new devices in 90 minutes,
  cleared after about 30 minutes. podnet then says so. A saved identity,
  `warp rotate` and new sessions do not register. `--ephemeral`, a new
  `--listen-identity` file and `warp export` each register one device.
## Proxy

* `podnet warp proxy` listens on `tcp://127.0.0.1:40000` by default. Use
  `--listen unix:/path` on a host that refuses `AF_INET` binds. Each
  `--listen` is bound on its own: a listener that the host refuses is
  reported, and the proxy starts with the others (`--strict` exits 69
  instead). With no listener, the exit code is 69. Names are resolved
  through the tunnel. A pin of `--resolve HOST=IP` or `PODNET_RESOLVE`
  comes first and sends no query. This applies also to `warp forward` and
  `warp nc`. SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE is supported.
* `--proxy-user USER --proxy-password-file FILE` (also on `warp up`): each
  client must give the user and the password of the first line of FILE
  (mode 0600), with SOCKS5 (RFC 1929) or HTTP `Proxy-Authorization: Basic`.
  A listener on an address that is not loopback, with no credentials, gets
  a warning. `--max-connections N` limits the clients; `--dns ADDR`
  answers DNS through WARP.
## Transports and carriers

* `--fragment-client-hello [off|record|sni]` (default `off`; a flag of `podnet warp`, before or after the subcommand; `PODNET_WARP_FRAGMENT`):
  the TLS ClientHello of the MASQUE connection goes in more than one record
  of `--fragment-size` bytes (16 to 4096; default 64-160). `sni` ends the first record in the
  server name. The server joins the records (RFC 8446, section 5.1); a
  middlebox that reads the name from the first record does not find it.
* `--carry wg` (a flag of `podnet warp`, before or after the subcommand; `PODNET_WARP_CARRY`): a second WireGuard device
  (`warp-carry.json` in the state directory) inside the tunnel, on a UDP
  socket of the first stack. The tools use the stack of the second device
  (IPv4, MTU 1200), so a destination sees its exit. With `--transport
  wireguard`, both hops are WireGuard. Not for `warp tun`.
* `warp proxy --l4` (`PODNET_WARP_L4`): each TCP client is one HTTP/3
  `CONNECT` stream to the L4 door of WARP (UDP 443, TLS name of `--l4-sni`,
  `consumer-masque-proxy.cloudflareclient.com`), with no IP stack in
  between. UDP (SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE) is not served. The rules apply (`-r`,
  `--rules-file`, `--rule-default`): a `cidr:` rule decides an address, and a
  name with no other rule takes `--rule-default`.
* `--transport wireguard` (a flag of `podnet warp`, before or after the subcommand; `PODNET_WARP_TRANSPORT`): the tunnel on
  WireGuard (UDP, port 2408 of the record, or `--wireguard-endpoint`) in
  place of MASQUE. The device is the one of `podnet warp export`
  (`warp-wg.json` in the state directory); podnet registers it when the file
  has none. The stack, the proxy and the commands are the same. There is no
  relay and no proxy: WireGuard is UDP.
* The reserved bytes: WARP reads bytes 1 to 3 of each WireGuard message,
  the `client_id` of the device (`# Reserved = a,b,c` in the output of
  `warp export`, `reserved` in the JSON form). Kernel WireGuard and
  wg-quick send zeros there. `--transport wireguard` sends the bytes. A
  device that needs them has fresh handshakes and no data path in kernel
  WireGuard. `podnet warp export --check` runs the WireGuard leg of podnet
  with the bytes and with zeros, with a TCP connect to the target of
  `--probe` through each. It prints `device ok` (exit 0), `needs reserved
  bytes` (exit 1) or `device data path dead, use --new` (exit 69). The
  TCP probe of `--probe` also runs on the stack of `--transport
  wireguard`: a leg with fresh handshakes and no TCP gets a new session.
* `--masque-transport h3` (a flag of `podnet warp`, before or after the subcommand; `PODNET_WARP_MASQUE_TRANSPORT`): the MASQUE
  session over HTTP/3 on UDP 443 in place of HTTP/2 on TCP 443. Each IP
  packet is an HTTP datagram (RFC 9297), so a lost packet does not stop the
  other flows. A packet larger than a datagram goes as a capsule on the
  request stream. There is no relay and no proxy: they carry TCP only.
* `--cc none|reno|cubic` (a flag of `podnet warp`, before or after the subcommand; `PODNET_WARP_CC`): the congestion
  controller of the TCP connections of the userspace stack, for the data
  that it sends (an upload). The default is `none`: only the window of the
  peer limits it.
## Listeners, identities and rules

* `--listen-identity LISTEN=PATH` (repeatable): the clients of LISTEN use
  the WARP device of the identity file PATH (podnet makes it when it does not
  exist), with a session of its own and its own address. The `--listen`
  listeners use `--identity`. One file is for one listener only. The ready
  document lists the listeners and their devices in `identities`.
* Rules of `warp proxy` (`-r KIND:VALUE=ACTION`, repeatable): KIND is
  `domain` (`NAME`, or `.NAME` for the name and the names under it) or
  `cidr` (`ADDR/PREFIX`, IPv4 or IPv6, or `@FILE` with one prefix on each
  line, for example the prefixes of a country). ACTION is `tunnel`,
  `direct` (from the host, with the resolver of the host and no proxy) or
  `reject` (SOCKS5 reply 0x02, HTTP 403). The first rule that matches wins.
  A name that no domain rule matches is resolved through the tunnel when a
  cidr rule exists. Then a loopback, a link-local or an unspecified address
  and `localhost` are refused, then `--rule-default` (`tunnel`) applies.
  `--rules-file FILE` adds the rules of FILE (one on each line, `#` starts a
  comment); podnet reads it again when it changes and keeps the rules before
  when it has an error. `--check` prints the rules and exits. The rules
  apply to TCP; UDP goes through the tunnel. The health line counts the
  decisions.

  ```sh
  podnet warp proxy -r domain:.corp.example=direct -r cidr:10.0.0.0/8=direct \
      -r domain:.ads.example=reject --rules-file ~/.config/podnet/rules
  ```
## Run a program

* `podnet warp run --backend netns-raw` runs the program in a user and network
  namespace whose TUN goes to WARP as raw IP packets: TCP, UDP, ICMP and
  IPv6, with the kernel stack of the namespace and no root. The TUN has the
  WARP addresses and the default routes, and the program gets a
  `resolv.conf` with 1.1.1.1. `--backend auto` takes it when this host can
  make the namespace (and no `-r` rule is given), else the pod ([pods.md](pods.md)).
* `podnet warp run` starts the proxy on a unix socket and runs the program with
  `podnet pod` (`auto` takes the `seccomp` backend first, for UDP). It passes
  `-r` (for example `-r cidr:10.0.0.0/8=direct`), `--keep-proxy-env` and
  `--inbound-dir` to the pod. A connect to 127.0.0.1 goes to the host, not
  to WARP. The TCP connections and the DNS queries of the program go
  through WARP, also for static binaries. With the `seccomp` backend, other
  UDP datagrams also go through WARP (SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE). ICMP (`ping`)
  goes through WARP only with `--backend netns-raw`; the pod does not carry
  it.
* `podnet warp up [--port 40000] [--persist]` starts `warp proxy` in the
  background (instance `warp`, see [background.md](background.md)) on
  `127.0.0.1:PORT` and on a unix socket, and writes an env file with the
  proxy variables. When the host refuses the TCP listener, `warp up` starts
  with the socket only: the env file has no proxy variables, `warp env` says
  so and exits 69 with no output, and `warp exec` and `warp shell` work. Later shells join it:
  * `eval "$(podnet warp env)"`: `ALL_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`,
    `NO_PROXY` (and the lower-case forms), `CARGO_HTTP_PROXY` and the npm
    variables. The proxy also forwards `http://` URLs (for apt).
  * `podnet warp exec -- CMD` and `podnet warp shell`: the command runs under
    the pod of the socket: TCP, DNS and UDP go through WARP, also for static
    binaries, with no proxy variable. `--backend auto|netns|seccomp` selects
    the backend of the pod (default `auto`: netns first, then seccomp when
    the user namespace or the TUN fails). The pod writes one line on stderr
    that names the backend that runs, its limits and the reason of the
    choice; `-q` removes the line. With `-v`, the pod logs each flow, and
    the seccomp backend logs each socket and each `setsockopt` that it
    emulates.
  * `podnet warp exec --detach --name N -- CMD`: the pod is an instance
    (see [background.md](background.md)). It lives until each process of the pod
    ends, also a daemon that CMD starts (`rad node start`). `podnet ps`
    lists it, `podnet logs N` shows the output of the pod, and
    `podnet stop N` sends SIGTERM to each process of the pod (SIGKILL after
    5 s). The supervisor starts the pod again when it ends; `--no-restart`
    turns it off. `--name N` with no `--detach` runs the pod in the
    foreground as the instance N.
  * `podnet warp exec --join N -- CMD`: CMD runs in the pod of the instance
    N. It reaches the loopback listeners of the pod N, and a name gets the
    address that the pod N gave it. With the netns backend, CMD enters the
    namespaces of the pod N. With the seccomp backend, a new pod shares the
    inbound listeners and the fake DNS table of the pod N
    (`--session $RUN/N.pod` of `podnet pod`). `podnet stop N` does not stop
    CMD.
  * `--persist`: a marked block in `~/.bashrc` and `~/.profile` loads the env
    file in each new shell, and an interactive shell runs under the pod.
  * `--env-d`: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/environment.d/90-podnet-warp.conf`
    (`~/.config/environment.d/...` when the variable is not set) has the proxy
    variables. The systemd user manager gives them to the programs of the
    next login (a desktop, a browser, a user unit). A file of that name that
    podnet did not write stays, and `warp up --env-d` stops with an error.
  * `podnet warp down` stops the instance and removes the env file and the
    blocks (and the environment.d file of podnet); the rest of each file
    stays.
  * The CA bundle: when `SSL_CERT_FILE`, `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`,
    `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` or `GIT_SSL_CAINFO` names a bundle of fewer than 10
    certificates (the roots of a proxy that terminates TLS), the tools that
    use it fail through WARP, which shows the real chains. `warp up` then
    writes `warp-ca.pem` (that bundle and the system bundle) and the env
    file, `warp exec` and `warp shell` name it, so that the proxy and WARP
    both work. With no system bundle, a warning says to unset the variable.
## SSH over WARP

* `podnet warp nc HOST PORT`: a byte pipe from stdin and stdout to HOST:PORT
  through the running `podnet warp up` (else a WARP session of its own), for
  `ssh -o ProxyCommand='podnet warp nc %h %p'` and git over SSH where port 22
  is closed. `--via-relay` goes through the WebSocket relay to HOST:PORT
  with no WARP. `podnet warp ssh-config [--host PATTERN]` prints the SSH
  config block and a `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`. SSH checks the host key as on a
  direct connection. At the end of stdin, podnet sends no FIN: the pipe ends
  when the far end closes, or `--idle` seconds (default 5) after the last
  data. `-N` sends the FIN at the end of stdin, for a server that waits for
  it. An error of the far end exits 69.
* `podnet warp ssh-config --write --host github.com` puts the block in
  `~/.ssh/config` (or `--config FILE`), between two marker lines, before
  the first `Host` or `Match` line. A second `--write` replaces it (for
  example after podnet moved). `--check` exits 1 when the block is missing or
  stale; `--remove [--host PATTERN]` removes it. No other line of the file
  changes. A `Host` line of the file with the same pattern is an error, and
  the files of `Include` are not read. `podnet warp down` keeps the block.
  `--host` is one pattern of 1 to 255 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -
  * ? ! : @ % , [ ]`; a space, a newline or another control character
  exits 64, and nothing is printed or written.
## TUN interface

* `podnet warp tun --default-route` (CAP_NET_ADMIN) sends the whole host
  through WARP: a host route keeps each address of the MASQUE connection
  (the proxy, the front door, the relay) outside the TUN when the TUN
  would capture it. An address on loopback or on a connected subnet needs
  none, so a host with no default route works when its proxy is there; an
  address with no route at all is refused with its name. `0.0.0.0/1`,
  `128.0.0.0/1`, `::/1` and `8000::/1` go to the TUN; DNS goes to 1.1.1.1
  (`resolvectl` on the TUN, else `/etc/resolv.conf` with a copy kept). The
  default routes go away while the session is down, so traffic fails fast.
  The end (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, `podnet stop`) puts back each route and the
  resolver. The changes are ioctls; no script runs as root.
  `podnet warp up --tun` starts it detached (instance `warp-tun`), and
  `podnet warp down` stops it.
* `podnet warp tun` makes a TUN interface with the tunnel address and moves its
  packets through WARP. It does not change the routes: add routes for the
  destinations to send through WARP, and keep a route for the MASQUE endpoint
  outside the interface. The command prints examples.
## Sessions, relay and the registration API

* `podnet warp proxy`, `podnet warp run` and `podnet warp tun` open a new MASQUE
  session when the session ends (a network change, the front door, the
  limit of a relay): at once, then with a backoff of 1 s doubled to 30 s.
  A new client takes the new session; a client that comes while the
  session is down waits for it (20 s at most). `warp tun` keeps its
  interface. The log has `a new WARP session is open` for each.
* When the direct MASQUE path fails (a proxy that refuses CONNECT to an
  IP address, or that answers and carries nothing), podnet opens the same
  MASQUE TLS through the WebSocket relay of `--relay` (default
  `https://tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev`, see [tunnels.md](tunnels.md), "Edge protocol and transport"). The
  client certificate and the pinned key stay end to end. The path that
  worked goes first at the next session. `--no-relay` turns this off.
  `--masque-endpoint IP:PORT` and `--masque-sni NAME` replace the front
  door and its TLS name.
* `--resolver SPEC` (repeatable; `PODNET_WARP_RESOLVERS`): the resolver of the DNS inside the tunnel, in
  place of `1.1.1.1:53`. `SPEC` is `IP[:PORT]` (UDP) or `tls://IP[:PORT][#NAME]` (DNS over TLS, port 853;
  the certificate must have `NAME`, or the IP address). The first resolver that answers wins.
* `--device-name NAME` (1 to 64 characters), `--device-model MODEL` (default `PC`) and `--device-locale
  LOCALE` (default `en_US`; `PODNET_WARP_DEVICE_NAME`, `PODNET_WARP_DEVICE_MODEL`,
  `PODNET_WARP_DEVICE_LOCALE`) set what a new device declares to the WARP service.
* `--wireguard-endpoint IP:PORT` (`PODNET_WARP_WG_ENDPOINT`) replaces the WireGuard front door of the device
  record (port 2408). `--carry-endpoint IP:PORT` (`PODNET_WARP_CARRY_ENDPOINT`) replaces the front door of
  the carried device.
* The registration API calls and the MASQUE connection use the proxy (see
  [proxies.md](proxies.md)). A proxy that terminates TLS cannot carry the MASQUE
  connection, because the connection uses a client certificate.

<!-- document: docs/pods.md -->

# Pods: `podnet pod`

This page gives `podnet pod`: run a program with all its network traffic sent through an upstream. The
backends are in the library `crates/podnet-netns` (`crates/podnet-netns/README.md`).

`podnet pod` runs a program with all its
network traffic sent through a SOCKS5, HTTP or tailnet upstream. It does not
use `LD_PRELOAD`, so static binaries and Go binaries are also covered.

```sh
podnet pod -x socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 -- curl https://example.com
podnet pod -x http://proxy:3128 -- git clone https://example.com/repo
podnet pod -x socks5://unix:/run/proxy.sock -- ./static-binary
podnet pod -- curl https://example.com        # upstream from $ALL_PROXY or $HTTPS_PROXY
podnet pod doctor                             # which backend can run here
```

Two backends are available. `--backend auto` (the default) selects one.

| Backend | Needs | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `netns` | unprivileged user namespaces, and `/dev/net/tun` or a veth pair | The program gets a network namespace. A TUN device (else a veth pair) is its only interface. A userspace TCP/IP stack sends each flow to the upstream. |
| `seccomp` | seccomp with `SECCOMP_RET_USER_NOTIF` | A seccomp filter stops the socket system calls. The supervisor answers them and gives the program connected descriptors. |

Both backends answer DNS from a fake-IP pool (`198.18.0.0/15`; the
`seccomp` backend answers AAAA from `fd63:6672:7300::/96` too) and send the
name to the upstream. Thus no DNS query leaves the host. With the `netns`
backend, `--host-gateway` lets the program reach a service on the loopback
of the host at the gateway `10.66.255.254` (TCP and UDP, as the gateway of
podman and slirp4netns); without it, the gateway refuses. See
[`crates/podnet-netns/README.md`](../crates/podnet-netns/README.md) for all options.

## Upstreams

`-x SPEC` (or `--proxy SPEC`, or `--egress SPEC`) gives an upstream. It is repeatable: more than one `-x`
makes a chain, in the order given. Without `-x`, the upstream comes from `$ALL_PROXY`, `$HTTPS_PROXY` or
`$HTTP_PROXY`. A pod with no upstream is a usage error (exit 64).

* `socks5://[user:pass@]host:port` and `http://[user:pass@]host:port`.
* `socks5://unix:/path` and `http://unix:/path` (also `socks5h+unix:/path` and `http+unix:/path`): a proxy
  on a unix socket.
* `tailscale:/path/to/tailscaled.sock`: a tailnet ([networks.md](networks.md)).
* `wg:FILE` is not a hop of a pod. Run `podnet route` with a `wg:FILE` network, and give its door to `-x`.
* `netbird:[PORT]` through `--egress` (a SOCKS5 hop on `127.0.0.1:PORT`; [networks.md](networks.md)).
* `--serve LISTEN` runs no program. It serves SOCKS5, HTTP CONNECT and UDP ASSOCIATE on `unix:/path` or
  `tcp://host:port`, and sends the flows through the chain. It is the front door of
  [proxies.md](proxies.md), over the chain and the rules. UDP ASSOCIATE and UDP in the stream go
  through the first upstream, which must be SOCKS5. BIND gets `0x07`. `--early-reply` answers a CONNECT
  before the dial (see [proxies.md](proxies.md), "Early reply").

By default the program does not get `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY`.
`--keep-proxy-env` keeps them.

## Rules

`-r SPEC` (`--rule`) sends a destination its own way. The first rule that matches wins.

```sh
podnet pod -x socks5://127.0.0.1:1080 \
  -r domain:.corp.example=socks5://10.0.0.1:1080 \
  -r cidr:10.0.0.0/8=direct \
  -r domain:.ads.example=reject -- ./program
```

* `domain:NAME=WAY` matches a name. `domain:.NAME=WAY` matches the name and each name under it.
* `cidr:ADDR/PREFIX=WAY` matches an address.
* `WAY` is an upstream (`socks5://host:port`), `direct` (no proxy) or `reject` (or `block`). A rejected
  connect fails with `ECONNREFUSED` (netns: a reset). A rejected datagram gets `EACCES` (netns: it is
  dropped). `--serve` answers SOCKS5 `0x02` or HTTP 403.
* A rule that an earlier rule shadows (it can never match) gives a warning. A shadowed `reject` rule is an
  error (exit 64). `--allow-shadowed-rules` makes it a warning.
* `--default-action allow|reject` sets what the pod does with a target that no rule matches (default
  `allow`).
* With the `seccomp` backend, `127.0.0.0/8` goes direct (or to a listener of the program itself).
  `--loopback-rules` applies the rules to a TCP connect to `127.0.0.0/8` and `::1` too.

## Audit

* `--flow-log FILE` appends one JSON line to FILE for each decision (time, target, rule or default, chain,
  verdict) and one at the close of each relayed TCP flow (`bytes_out`, `bytes_in`).
* `--learn FILE` writes each destination of the run to FILE, one `PROTO TARGET` line each. A flow that a
  rule refuses goes through the `-x` chain.
* `--fail-on-violation FILE` refuses each destination that is not in FILE (a file of `--learn`). A learned
  destination that a rule refuses is also a violation. The pod writes each violation on stderr and exits 4
  when the program exits 0.

## Other options

* `--backend auto|netns|seccomp`; `--prefer-udp` (with `auto`: `seccomp` first when it works, because
  `netns` carries a datagram of 1500 bytes at most); `--name-backend` prints one line on stderr with the
  backend, its limits and the reason of the choice.
* `--map NAME=ADDR` resolves NAME to ADDR locally (repeatable).
* `--host-gateway` (netns): a connect to `10.66.255.254` and a port goes to `127.0.0.1` on the host.
* `--inbound-dir DIR` (seccomp): where a bound port is exposed as a unix socket. The directory must be of
  this user and not writable by the group or by others. The default is
  `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podnet-netns-inbound`, else `$TMPDIR/podnet-netns-inbound-UID`.
* `--session DIR` (seccomp): share the inbound listeners and the fake DNS table with each pod of DIR.
  `podnet warp exec --join` uses it ([warp.md](warp.md)).
* `--flow-budget N` (seccomp): the most sockets that the pod tracks at one time (64 to 1048576). A socket
  call above it gets `EMFILE`. The default comes from `RLIMIT_NOFILE`.
* A pod holds the traffic of the program. The `netns` backend enforces it, except unix sockets of the file
  system and the descriptors that the program inherits. The `seccomp` backend is advisory: unix, netlink,
  vsock, raw and packet sockets, loopback TCP and inherited descriptors are not held.
* Exit status: the exit code of the program; 64 for a usage mistake (also no upstream); 3 when no backend
  can run on this host; 4 for a violation of `--fail-on-violation` when the program exits 0.

## Check the host: `podnet pod doctor`

`podnet pod doctor [--json]` measures what the host permits and says which backend can run
([doctor.md](doctor.md)). It exits 3 when no backend can run. When a program and WARP are the goal, use
`podnet warp run` and `podnet warp exec` ([warp.md](warp.md)): they run a pod over WARP.

<!-- document: docs/networks.md -->

# Virtual networks and overlays

This page gives `podnet net`: the virtual network, Tailscale, NetBird, WireGuard and the passwd shim. The design
of the virtual network is in [virtual-network.md](virtual-network.md). The specs `tailscale:`, `netbird:` and
`wg:` are networks of the registry ([egress.md](egress.md)).

| Command | Function |
| --- | --- |
| `net demo` | Prove a userspace TCP handshake and a transfer in the process. |
| `net doctor` | Probe what this host permits ([doctor.md](doctor.md)). |
| `net addresses` | Print the default virtual address plan. |
| `net shim` | Build or find the `LD_PRELOAD` shim and print how to use it. |
| `net proxy` | Run a SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT proxy into the virtual network. |
| `net switch` | Run a switch that connects stacks on this host and on other hosts. |
| `net tailscale` | A SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT front door to a tailnet through `tailscaled`. |
| `net socksify` | Build the shim that sends tailnet connects to a front door. |
| `net passwd-shim`, `net ts-shims` | Files for a user with no passwd entry. |

## Virtual network: `podnet net`

`podnet net` gives programs IP addresses on a host that refuses `AF_INET` binds.
It needs no namespace, no TUN device and no capability.

```sh
podnet net doctor                         # what this host permits
podnet net shim --out /tmp/podnet-vnet        # build the LD_PRELOAD shim
LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/podnet-vnet/libpodnet-vnet.so ./server      # bind 10.66.0.2:8080 works
podnet net proxy --forward 10.66.0.2:8080=unix:/run/app.sock
podnet net switch --listen unix:/tmp/podnet-vnet.switch   # connect stacks
podnet net proxy --switch unix:/tmp/podnet-vnet.switch --address 10.66.0.3
```

`net proxy` is the front door of [proxies.md](proxies.md) over the stack. The door
answers a closed virtual port with 502 (SOCKS5 `0x04`), and an address that nothing owns with 504 after 5 s.

A unix switch takes the same user only. A TCP switch needs a shared token:
set `PODNET_SWITCH_TOKEN`, or give `--switch-token-file PATH`, to the switch
and to each `net proxy --switch tcp://...`. With no token, the switch does
not start (exit 64). A peer with no token or a wrong one is closed. The
switch drops a packet whose source address is of another peer.

```sh
export PODNET_SWITCH_TOKEN="$(head -c 24 /dev/urandom | base64)"
podnet net switch --listen tcp://0.0.0.0:7000
podnet net proxy --switch tcp://switch-host:7000 --address 10.66.0.3
```

`podnet net doctor` calls `bind` and then `listen` for each stream socket
(a policy can allow one and refuse the other; `SO_ACCEPTCONN` confirms the
listen), and sends one QUIC packet to the edge on UDP 7844: answered, refused
or `?` (no answer in 3 s). It prints the commands that need each listener.
`PODNET_UDP=off` makes a tunnel use no QUIC on UDP 7844; `PODNET_UDP=on` skips
the probe at start.

See [virtual-network.md](virtual-network.md).

## Tailscale on a sealed host

```sh
podnet net tailscale --socket /run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock   # SOCKS5 front door to the tailnet
eval "$(podnet net socksify --socket /tmp/podnet-socks.sock)"     # shim for tailnet connects
podnet net ts-shims --out /run/podnet-ts-shims                   # user tables for Tailscale SSH
podnet pod -x tailscale:/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock -- ssh host
```

`tailscaled` must run with `--tun=userspace-networking`. The door of `net tailscale` is the front door of
[proxies.md](proxies.md) over `tailscaled`. A dial that `tailscaled` does not answer in 10 s gets
SOCKS5 `0x04` or HTTP 504.

`--tailnet NAME` (or `PODNET_TAILNET`) starts the door only when `tailscaled`
is `Running` in that tailnet. NAME is the tailnet name or its DNS suffix.
Another tailnet exits 78 and binds nothing. A daemon that is not logged in
after 20 s exits 69. While the door runs, it refuses new dials when the daemon
changes to another tailnet (SOCKS5 "connection not allowed", HTTP 403). Open
connections stay. `podnet net doctor [--socket PATH]` shows the state of the daemon: `ok` when it is
`Running`, `fail` when it is `NeedsLogin`, `Stopped` or another state, and `unknown` when the socket does not
answer.

The spec `tailscale:/PATH` is a network of the registry ([egress.md](egress.md)). It is a hop of `podnet pod -x`
and `--egress`, the `--network` of `podnet forward`, a network of a router file and a member of a group
([router.md](router.md)). It is the only hop of a chain. `podnet route --check` prints its login state. A
router that starts with a daemon that is not `Running` prints one warning, and the link of the network has the
`state` in its status. The name of the target goes to `tailscaled` (MagicDNS), so a name or an address of the tailnet works.

A host whose outbound traffic is limited to port 443 starts `tailscaled`
with `TS_FORCE_NOISE_443=true`. Without it, the control connection tries port
80 first, and a middlebox can accept that connection and stall.

`net socksify --cidr ROUTE` routes only the listed destinations to the door
(repeatable: `tailnet`, `ADDR`, `ADDR/BITS`, `IPV4:PORT` or `[IPV6]:PORT`),
for example a client with the fixed origin `127.0.0.1:3000`. `net shim
--socks-route ROUTE` does the same in the shim of the virtual network. See
[virtual-network.md](virtual-network.md),
section 5.5.

## NetBird in netstack mode

NetBird joins a host with no TUN device in netstack mode. The daemon then
gives a SOCKS5 listener on `127.0.0.1`.

```sh
NB_USE_NETSTACK_MODE=true NB_SOCKS5_LISTENER_PORT=1080 NB_SETUP_KEY=... netbird up -F
podnet pod -x netbird:1080 -- ssh 100.64.0.7        # the peer by its NetBird IP address
podnet net doctor                                    # the row "NetBird (SOCKS5 listener)"
```

The network spec is `netbird:[PORT]` (default 1080). It dials the SOCKS5
listener at `127.0.0.1:PORT`. podnet does not start the daemon. The spec
gives TCP only. It takes the IP address of a peer. A host name fails with one
line, because netstack mode has no DNS. The listener has no authentication:
keep it on `127.0.0.1`. The doctor row sends a SOCKS5 greeting to the port
(`NB_SOCKS5_LISTENER_PORT`, else 1080). A listener that does not answer is
`unknown`, not a fault.

## WireGuard: `wg:FILE`

```sh
podnet forward --network wg:/etc/wireguard/wg0.conf -L 127.0.0.1:8080=10.9.0.1:80
```

The spec `wg:FILE` makes a WireGuard peer a network. `FILE` is a wg-quick file with one peer
(`PrivateKey`, `Address`, `MTU`; `PublicKey`, `Endpoint`, `Reserved`). podnet does the handshake itself and
runs a userspace stack over the tunnel. It makes no TUN device and needs no capability. The spec gives TCP and
UDP from the `Address` of the file.

* The target must be an IP address. The network does not resolve names.
* A file with a `PresharedKey` is refused with one line.
* `up` does the handshake. A path with no UDP gives no answer in 15 s, and the error says that the UDP path
  may be closed.
* The UDP of the tunnel goes out from this host. A way below the network (`Ctx::below`, a layer of a chain)
  can carry it instead. That way must carry UDP (`Dial::datagrams`). The status of the link names it in
  `carrier`. A way that carries no UDP, a proxy for example, is refused with `carries no UDP`.
* `wg:FILE` is a network of `podnet forward --network` and of a `networks:` entry of a router file
  ([router.md](router.md)). It is not a hop of `podnet pod` (T-117): run `podnet route` with the network and
  give its door to `-x`.
* The WARP datagram path (MASQUE CONNECT-IP) is not a carrier of the registry (T-117), because `warp` is not a
  network of the registry ([egress.md](egress.md)).

## A user with no passwd entry

On a host where `/etc/passwd` has no entry for your uid, `getpwuid` fails.
Then `ssh` stops, and `ssh-keygen` exits 0 and writes no key. `podnet net
doctor` shows the row `passwd entry for this uid`. `podnet net passwd-shim`
writes a passwd file and the preload `fakepwd.so`, and prints `LD_PRELOAD`
(before an old value) and `SANDHOME_PASSWD`:

```sh
eval "$(podnet net passwd-shim)"
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 -N ''
```

`--user`, `--uid`, `--gid` and `--shell` set the entry. `--json` prints the
environment as one object. `net ts-shims` writes the same files, with
`getent` and `id`, and prints the hints for `tailscaled`.

<!-- document: docs/router.md -->

# Router: `podnet route`

`podnet route --config FILE` runs a router from a YAML file. The router has networks, groups of
networks, health probes, policies and doors. A door is a SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT listener. A guest wire lets a guest use the router as its gateway. Each flow
that comes to a door goes out through the network or the group that the door names. The kernel mode
writes policy routing for WANs, with no `ip` program.

The router needs no root, no TUN device and no namespace, except the kernel mode, which needs
`CAP_NET_ADMIN`. A guest wire (below) needs a unix socket, or a TUN device that exists.

```sh
podnet route --config router.yml                        # run in the foreground
podnet route --config router.yml --detach --name edge   # run in the background
podnet route --config router.yml --check                # read the file and bring up nothing
podnet route --config router.yml --check --to example.com:443   # a dry run for one target
podnet route --status unix:/run/r.ctl                   # the state of a running router
podnet route --status unix:/run/r.ctl --json
podnet route --status unix:/run/r.ctl --metrics         # the rows of the metrics (Prometheus text)
podnet route --control unix:/run/r.ctl --select egress=proxy    # pin a group to one member
podnet route --control unix:/run/r.ctl --select egress=auto     # give the choice back to the policy
podnet route --control unix:/run/r.ctl --rotate proxy           # a new identity of a network
podnet route --control unix:/run/r.ctl --reconnect proxy        # a new link, the same identity
podnet route --control unix:/run/r.ctl --interval 5             # seconds between two probes
podnet route --config router.yml --export mwan-json     # the WANs of the kernel section as JSON
```

## The file

```yaml
networks:                 # NAME: SPEC (see egress.md)
  home: direct
  proxy: socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080
groups:                   # NAME: MEMBER*WEIGHT, MEMBER*WEIGHT, ...
  egress: home*2, proxy*1
policies:                 # optional, NAME: POLICY of a group
  egress: minrtt
splits:                   # optional, NAME: up=MEMBER down=MEMBER of a group
  egress: up=home down=proxy
health:                   # the probe of the members of each group
  target: 1.1.1.1:443
  interval: 10
  down_after: 4
  up_after: 3
  cooldown: 30
  timeout: 5
  window: 8
  egress:                 # optional: the egress check of a network (see below)
    proxy: 203.0.113.9:7=198.51.100.4
resolvers:                # optional: NETWORK: HOST:PORT, a DNS server at the far end of the network
  proxy: 10.0.0.53:53
control: unix:/run/r.ctl  # optional: the socket of `route --status` and `--control`
state_dir: /var/lib/r     # optional: DIR/NETWORK holds the identity of a network
doors:
  - listen: unix:/run/r.sock    # HOST:PORT, tcp://HOST:PORT or unix:/PATH
    via: egress                 # a network or a group of the file
    rules: /etc/r.rules         # optional: rules that go before `via`
    allow_shadowed_rules: false
    dns: 127.0.0.1:5353         # optional: a DNS door over the same way
    dns_upstream: 10.0.0.53:53  # the resolver at the far end (needed with dns)
```

* The file uses the YAML reader of podnet (block mappings and sequences, comments; no flow collections
  except `[]` and `{}`). An unknown key is a usage error (exit 64, with or without `--check`), and the
  error names the key or the line.
* A name is letters, digits, `-` and `_`. A group and a network cannot have the same name.
* `networks` maps a name to a network spec (see [egress.md](egress.md)): `direct`, a proxy URL, `relay`,
  `tailscale:/PATH`, `netbird:[PORT]`, `wg:FILE` or `unix:/PATH`. A `tailscale:/PATH` network is a member of a group
  and the `via` of a door, as each other network. When `tailscaled` is not `Running` at the start, the
  router prints one warning and goes on: each dial through that network fails until the daemon is logged
  in.
* `groups` maps a name to a list of members. A member is a network name with an optional weight
  (`home*2`). The default weight is 1.
* The file needs one door or more, unless it has a `guests` entry or a `kernel` section. A file with `kernel` needs no door.
* A flow takes one member and never moves to another.

## Doors

* A door accepts SOCKS5 (CONNECT and UDP ASSOCIATE) and HTTP CONNECT.
* UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928) carries the datagrams of a client over the datagrams of the network or the
  group of the door. The door answers with a UDP socket on its own address (the address of `listen`;
  the loopback address for a `unix:` door). The first datagram fixes the source of the client; a datagram
  of another source and a fragment are dropped. An answer goes back only from an address that the client
  sent to. The association ends when the client closes the control connection, or after 300 s with no
  datagram. A name in a datagram resolves with the resolver of this host (the datagrams of a network take
  an address). The reply is 0x07 (command not supported) when the network carries no UDP (a SOCKS5 or
  HTTP proxy), and 0x02 (not allowed) when the group has no member that takes flows. The bytes count
  for the member that carries the socket. The rules of the door choose by the target of a CONNECT only:
  a UDP association goes over `via`.
* `via` names the network or the group for a target that no rule matches.
* `rules` is a rules file. A rule is `domain:NAME=WAY`, `domain:.NAME=WAY` (the name and each name under
  it), `cidr:NET=WAY` or `cidr:@FILE=WAY` (one prefix on each line of FILE). `WAY` is a network or a
  group of the router, or `reject` (or `block`). The first rule that matches wins. `#` starts a comment.
  podnet reads the file again when it changes. A rule that an earlier rule shadows gives a warning; a
  shadowed `reject` rule is an error, and the file does not load unless the door has
  `allow_shadowed_rules: true`.
* `dns` and `dns_upstream` start a DNS door (UDP and TCP) on `dns`. It sends each query over the same
  way as the door, to the resolver `dns_upstream` at the far end of the way. The router names no resolver
  of its own, so give both keys or none.
* `resolvers` gives a network a DNS server at the far end of the network: `NETWORK: HOST:PORT`. A name
  that a flow brings to a member of that network resolves there, with DNS over TCP (RFC 7766) over the
  dial of the member, and never with the resolver of this host. A, then AAAA, are asked over one
  connection; IPv4 addresses go first, and the flow tries up to 8 addresses. A name that the network
  cannot resolve is an error: there is no fallback to the host. A network whose far end resolves names
  (a `socks5h://` proxy, `relay`) gets the name as it is, and needs no entry. A flow that has an address
  needs no query.

## Guest wires

A guest (a VM, a container, a host behind one wire) uses the router as its gateway. The wire carries IPv4
packets. A userspace stack ends the TCP and the UDP of the guest, and the router sends each flow to a network
or a group, as it does for a door.

```yaml
guests:
  - wire: unix:/run/g.sock    # unix:/PATH or tun:NAME
    net: 10.66.0.0/24         # the guest net
    via: egress               # a network or a group of the file
    rules: /etc/r.rules       # optional: rules that go before `via`
    allow_shadowed_rules: false
    mtu: 1500                 # optional, 576 to 9000
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `wire` | `unix:/PATH`: the router listens on a `SOCK_SEQPACKET` socket (mode 0600). Each message is one IPv4 packet. One guest is connected at a time; a new connection replaces the old one. `tun:NAME`: the router opens the TUN device `NAME`, which must exist or be allowed (`CAP_NET_ADMIN`). The operator sets its address and routes. |
| `net` | `A.B.C.D/N`, N from 8 to 30. The router is the first host of the net (the gateway of the guest). |
| `via`, `rules`, `allow_shadowed_rules` | As for a door. |
| `mtu` | The MTU of the wire. Default 1500. Set it to the MTU of the guest. |

* The router drops a packet whose source is outside `net`, whose destination is in `net`, a multicast,
  broadcast, loopback or link-local address, or whose protocol is not TCP or UDP. IPv6 is dropped.
* TCP: the router holds the first SYN of a flow and dials the target (30 s limit) before the handshake. A dial
  that fails, or a rule that rejects, answers the SYN with a RST: `connect` of the guest fails at once. A copy of
  the SYN waits. At 2048 flows a new SYN is dropped, and the guest sends it again.
* UDP: each flow (guest address and target) has one socket from `Dial::datagrams` of the way that the rules
  choose, and takes one member of a group. A flow has a queue of 32 datagrams; a datagram for a full queue is
  dropped and counted. A flow ends after 60 s with no datagram. At most 512 flows and 256 ports. IPv4
  fragmentation (the feature `ipv4-fragmentation` of `pod-netstack`) carries a datagram over the MTU, up to
  65507 bytes.
* The guest resolves names itself (a flow to its resolver is a UDP or TCP flow), so a `domain:` rule does not
  match a flow of a guest. Use `cidr:` rules.
* `--status` shows each guest with its counters. The metrics have `podnet_route_guest_*` rows with the label
  `guest` (the wire): `tcp_dialed`, `tcp_refused`, `tcp_syn_dropped`, `tcp_open`, `udp_flows`, `udp_up`,
  `udp_down`, `udp_queue_dropped`, `udp_oversize`, `udp_refused` and `dropped`. The counters of the stack are
  `stack_udp_rx_dropped` (the backlog of a port was full), `stack_udp_tx_dropped` and `stack_udp_oversize`.
* `--check` prints a line for each guest.

## Groups, health and policies

The probe connects to `health.target` through each member of each group, each `interval` seconds
(default 10).

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `target` | none | `HOST:PORT` that each member must reach. |
| `interval` | 10 | Seconds between two probes. 1 or more. |
| `down_after` | 4 | K: the misses in a row that take a member down. |
| `up_after` | 3 | R: the passes in a row that take a member up. |
| `cooldown` | 30 | The least seconds in cooldown before a member is up again. |
| `timeout` | 5 | Seconds of one probe. 1 or more. |
| `window` | 8 | How many passing probe times the floor of `minrtt` reads (0 to 64). |
| `egress` | none | A map `NETWORK: HOST:PORT=IP`, the egress check of a network (below). |

The values must give K > R > 1 and R > K/2. A member in `cooldown` or `probation` is not up. A group
with no member that takes flows refuses new flows.

### Egress check

A probe that connects says that a network reaches the target. It does not say by which address the
traffic leaves. `egress` adds a check for the networks that it names. After the probe passes, the router
connects through the same member to `HOST:PORT`, an echo service of the operator, and reads at most 128
bytes. The service writes the address that it sees for the peer (an IP address, `IP:PORT` or `[IP]:PORT`,
then a new line or the end) and closes. The address must be the `IP` of the entry. podnet names no echo
service of another party: give one that you run or trust.

* The same address: the probe passes, and its time is the time of both connects.
* Another address: the result is `WrongEgress`. The member goes `down` at once, with no K misses, whatever
  the control probe says. No other way replaces it: the group has no direct way, so a group with no other
  member refuses its flows. One pass puts the member on `probation`, as after any `down`.
* An answer that is no address, or a read that fails: a miss that is not clean (as a time out), so it
  alone never takes the member down.

A WARP member has its own check (the trace request of the WARP session). It waits for `pod-warp`
(T-050).

A policy chooses the member of a new flow:

| Policy | Choice |
| --- | --- |
| `weighted` (default) | A random pick by weight. |
| `rr` | The members that take flows, in turn. The weights do not count. |
| `minrtt` | The head: the member with the least round-trip floor. The head changes only when another member is better by a margin (the larger of 5 ms and 10 percent) for 3 probe rounds. |
| `leastload` | The least busy member (by the bytes and the open flows, with a decay). |
| `protect` | A weighted pick among the members that are `up`. A member in `cooldown` or `probation` gets no flow while a member is `up`. |

`splits` sends the UDP datagrams of a group out through one member and receives them on another:
`NAME: up=MEMBER down=MEMBER`. It is off by default. TCP is not split. The byte meter of a member counts
TCP flows and UDP datagrams, in both directions. With a split, `up` counts the datagrams that it sends
and `down` counts the datagrams that it receives.

## Dry run: `--check --to`

`--check` reads the file and brings up no network. For each `tailscale:/PATH` network, it prints a line
`podnet: route  tailnet NAME: socket=PATH BackendState=... tailnet=...` after one read of the LocalAPI of
`tailscaled`. A daemon that is not `Running`, or that does not answer, gives the reason in that line; the
exit code does not change. It exits 0 when the file is valid, and 64 with the key
that is wrong.

`--check --to HOST:PORT` adds a dry run for one target. It prints, for each door (`--door INDEX` selects
one, counted from 0), the rule, the network or the group, the member and its health, and it dials
nothing. It exits 1 when a door refuses the target or when its group has no member that is up.

```text
door	listen	rule	way	member	health
0	unix:/run/r.sock	default	egress	home	up
```

## State: `--status`

A router with the key `control` serves a unix socket (mode 0600). `podnet route --status unix:/PATH`
prints the state of that router: each group, each member with its health, round-trip time and floor, the
flows, the bytes, the pinned member and the head. `--json` prints the document. Exit 69 when no router
answers. `--status` cannot be used with `--config`.

`podnet route --status unix:/PATH --metrics` prints the rows of the metrics in the text format of
Prometheus (it cannot be used with `--json`). There is one row for each member and metric, with the
labels `group` and `member`:

| Row | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `podnet_route_member_up` | gauge | 1 when the member is `up`; 0 in `cooldown`, on `probation` or `down`. |
| `podnet_route_member_takes_flows` | gauge | 1 when the member is not `down`. |
| `podnet_route_member_weight` | gauge | The weight of the member. |
| `podnet_route_member_rtt_seconds` | gauge | The time of the last probe that passed (no row before the first). |
| `podnet_route_member_rtt_floor_seconds` | gauge | The least time in the window of passing probes. |
| `podnet_route_member_open_dials` | gauge | The dials that have not ended. |
| `podnet_route_member_flows_total` | counter | The flows that the pick gave the member. |
| `podnet_route_member_bytes_total` | counter | The bytes of TCP and UDP, both directions. |
| `podnet_route_group_refused_total` | counter | The flows that the kill switch of the group refused (label `group` only). |

## Control: `--control`

`podnet route --control unix:/PATH` changes a running router with no restart. Flows that run go on. Give one of
these flags. Each prints the new state (`--json` for the JSON document).

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--select GROUP=MEMBER` | Pins the group to one member. Each new flow takes it, whatever the policy says. A pinned member that is down refuses the flows: the group does not fall back to another member or to direct. |
| `--select GROUP=auto` | Gives the choice back to the policy. |
| `--rotate MEMBER` | Makes a new identity of the network. The router brings up the new link first, gives it to the new flows, and ends the old link after 30 s (a flow on it can end before). The network keeps its state directory (`state_dir/NETWORK`), so it registers no new device. One rotate for each network and minute: a second one gets exit 75. Each rotate is logged on stderr. |
| `--reconnect MEMBER` | Makes a new link of the network with the same identity, make before break. |
| `--interval SECONDS` | Sets the seconds between two probes (1 to 86400). The wait of the probe ends at once. The file needs a `health` section. |

A `MEMBER` is a network of the file. A rotate or a reconnect reaches each group, rule and door that
uses the network. The networks of the registry (`direct`, a proxy, the relay) have no identity, so a
rotate makes a new link as a reconnect does. A network with an identity takes the rotate; WARP
becomes a network of the registry with the take of `pod-warp` (T-050).

The socket answers an HTTP/1.0 request with JSON. The gate is the mode 0600 of the socket and the user
of the peer: the user of the router, or root. A peer that is not allowed gets 403 and nothing changes.

| Request | Body |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /route/status` | none |
| `GET /route/metrics` | none; the answer is the text format of Prometheus, not JSON |
| `POST /route/select` | `{"group": "egress", "member": "proxy"}`; `"member": null` or `"auto"` frees the group |
| `POST /route/rotate` | `{"member": "proxy"}` |
| `POST /route/reconnect` | `{"member": "proxy"}` |
| `PATCH /route/interval` | `{"seconds": 5}` |

A write answers with the status document of the new state. An error answers `{"error": TEXT}` with
400 (a bad request), 403 (the gate), 404 (an unknown path, group or member), 405 (a wrong method), 409
(no `health` section), 429 (a rotate too soon) or 502 (the network did not come up; the way stays as it
was). The exit codes of the flags: 64 for 4xx, 75 for 429, 69 when no router answers.

## Kernel mode

The key `kernel` makes the router write policy routing with rtnetlink (no `ip` program). It needs
`CAP_NET_ADMIN`. At the end of the run, the router removes what it wrote.

```yaml
kernel:
  wans:
    - name: a            # letters, digits, - and _
      dev: tun0          # the interface of the WAN
      gateway: 10.0.0.1  # optional IPv4 next hop
      weight: 2          # 1 to 256 in the aggregate route (default 1)
      table: 101         # optional (default 100 + position)
      mark: 1            # optional fwmark (default 1 + position)
    - name: b
      dev: tun1
  table: 200             # the aggregate table (default 200)
  priority: 1000         # the priority of the first rule (default 1000)
  masquerade: true       # a masquerade on each WAN through nf_tables (default true)
  mss_clamp: true        # clamp the TCP MSS to the route MTU (default true)
  kill_switch: true      # an unreachable default route in the aggregate table (default true)
  rp_filter: true        # rp_filter 0 on each WAN (default true)
```

The plan has these rules, in this order of priority:

1. `lookup main suppress_prefixlength 0`: the routes of the local subnets win, and the default route of
   the main table does not.
2. `fwmark M lookup T` for each WAN: a marked packet leaves by its WAN.
3. `lookup AGGREGATE`: the other packets use the weighted multipath default route.

A change is made before the old state is broken: podnet writes the new routes with `NLM_F_REPLACE`, adds
the new rules, and then deletes the old rules that the new plan does not hold. There is no moment with no rule. With `kill_switch`, the aggregate table has an unreachable default route, so the traffic fails
when each WAN is down.

`podnet route --config FILE --export mwan-json` prints the WANs of the kernel section in the JSON form
of the mwan director (`wans` and `clients`) and runs nothing. It exits 64 when the file has no kernel
section.

## Background and autostart

`--detach --name NAME` runs the router as an instance (see [background.md](background.md)).
`podnet autostart add NAME -- route --config FILE` starts it at boot.

<!-- document: docs/forward.md -->

# Forwards, DNS door and `expose`

This page gives `podnet forward` (local ports that go out through a network), its DNS door, and
`podnet expose` (one word to publish a local service).

## `podnet forward`

`podnet forward -L LISTEN=HOST:PORT` listens on `LISTEN`. Each connection to it goes through a network to
`HOST:PORT`, as `ssh -L` does. No root and no TUN device are necessary.

```sh
podnet forward -L 5432=db.internal:5432                          # TCP, through the way out of the process
podnet forward --network socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 -L 8443=example.com:443
podnet forward --network tailscale:/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock -L 2222=host:22
podnet forward --network relay -L 2222=203.0.113.7:22
podnet forward -L udp:5353=10.0.0.53:53 --network socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080   # UDP
podnet forward --dns 127.0.0.1:5353 --dns-upstream 10.0.0.53:53              # a DNS door
podnet forward -L unix:/run/db.sock=db.internal:5432 --run-for 3600
```

* `-L, --local LISTEN=HOST:PORT` is repeatable. `LISTEN` is `PORT` (on 127.0.0.1), `ADDR:PORT`,
  `tcp://ADDR:PORT` or `unix:/PATH`.
* `-L LISTEN=peer:FINGERPRINT/SERVICE` opens one stream of a link to a peer for each accepted connection, and asks the peer
  for its service (see "A service of a peer" below). It carries TCP only.
* `--network SPEC` selects the network (see [egress.md](egress.md)): `direct`, a proxy URL, `relay` or
  `relay:URL`, `tailscale:/PATH`, `netbird:[PORT]`, `wg:FILE`, `unix:/PATH`. The default is the way out of the process: `--proxy`, the
  proxy variables, else direct.
* UDP: `-L udp:PORT=HOST:PORT` (or `udp:ADDR:PORT`) carries UDP over the datagrams of the network. Each
  client has its own flow. A flow ends after 60 s with no datagram. A datagram for a full flow is dropped.
  A SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy network carries no UDP: the forward logs the refusal and ends the flow. `direct`
  and `wg:FILE` carry UDP. A name in the target of a UDP forward resolves with the resolver of this host.
  For UDP through a door that clients choose (SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE) and for names that resolve inside a
  network, use the router ([router.md](router.md), "Doors" and `resolvers`).
* `--run-for SECONDS` stops after that time.

### A service of a peer

```sh
podnet link connect /run/user/1000/app.sock --peer FINGERPRINT --control /run/user/1000/link.ctl --detach --name peer1
export PODNET_LINK_CONTROL=/run/user/1000/link.ctl            # not needed when the instance is in the run directory
podnet forward -L 8080=peer:FINGERPRINT/http                  # 127.0.0.1:8080 -> the service http of the peer
podnet forward -L unix:/run/db.sock=peer:FINGERPRINT/db       # a unix listener
```

* A link instance (`podnet link connect`, or `link listen` for the links it accepts) holds the link and runs a control socket
  ([link.md](link.md)). The forward is another process: it asks that socket to open a stream. `PODNET_LINK_CONTROL` names one
  socket. Without it, the forward asks the control socket of each link instance in the run directory.
* The check runs before the forward listens. A link to a peer that is not the named `FINGERPRINT` exits 77, and no stream opens.
  No link instance that runs, or one with no link up, exits 69.
* Each accepted connection opens one new stream, and the first line of the stream names the service. The listener of the far side
  maps the name to a target (`link listen --service NAME=TARGET`, or `--to TARGET` for `raw`). A service that the peer does not
  have, or whose origin does not answer, closes that connection. The forward and the link stay up.
* `--network peer:...` is refused with exit 64: a peer way takes the form `-L LISTEN=peer:FINGERPRINT/SERVICE`.
* The services that a peer offers beyond `--service` (SOCKS5, HTTP proxy, and the other services of the link workstream) are
  separate work.

### DNS door

`--dns ADDR:PORT` answers DNS queries (UDP and TCP) on `ADDR:PORT`. podnet sends each query through the
network to the resolver `--dns-upstream HOST:PORT` (default `1.1.1.1:53`), which is an address at the far
end of the network. A program that uses the door as its resolver sends no query from this host.

A door of the router has the same function with the keys `dns` and `dns_upstream` ([router.md](router.md)).

### `warp forward`

`podnet warp forward -L LISTEN=HOST:PORT` forwards through WARP ([warp.md](warp.md)).
`podnet warp forward --list` lists the forwards of the detached instances. `podnet warp forward` is not
an alias of `podnet forward`: it has the options of `podnet warp`.

## `podnet connect`

`podnet connect URL -L LISTEN` forwards local sockets through the `--forward` endpoint of a quick tunnel
(see [tunnels.md](tunnels.md), "Raw streams through a quick tunnel").

## `podnet expose`

`podnet expose TARGET` publishes a local service. It runs another command for the way that `--via` selects:

| `--via` | Command that runs | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tunnel` (default) | `podnet tunnel` | A public URL on a Cloudflare tunnel ([tunnels.md](tunnels.md)). |
| `relay` | `podnet relay node` | A node of the reverse relay: operators connect with `podnet relay connect` ([relay.md](relay.md)). |
| `switch` | `podnet net proxy --forward` | A virtual address on a switch of the virtual network ([networks.md](networks.md)). |

* `TARGET` is an `http://` or `https://` URL, a port, `host:port`, `tcp://host:port` or `unix:/path`.
* `--as VIRT` (with `--via switch`) gives the virtual address of the service, as `VIRT` in
  `podnet net proxy --forward VIRT=REAL`, for example `10.66.0.2:8080`.
* The arguments after `--` go to the command that runs: for example `--detach`, a pair name or a
  `--switch`.

```sh
podnet expose 3000                                  # the same as podnet tunnel --port 3000
podnet expose 127.0.0.1:22 --via relay -- --detach
podnet expose unix:/run/app.sock --via switch --as 10.66.0.2:8080 -- --switch unix:/tmp/podnet-vnet.switch
```

<!-- document: docs/relay.md -->

# Relays: `podnet relay` and `podnet ssh-relay`

This page gives the reverse relay (`podnet relay`) and the SSH forward relay (`podnet ssh-relay`).

## Inbound access through the relay: `podnet relay`

A host with outbound HTTPS only cannot take inbound connections (SSH, a
debugger, a database client). A quick tunnel carries HTTP and WebSocket
only. The reverse mode of the WebSocket relay (`--relay`, default
`https://tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev`) carries raw TCP bytes to a local service.

```sh
# On the host:
podnet relay pair                                   # name, connect token; the node token stays in a 0600 file
podnet relay node --to 127.0.0.1:22 --detach        # hold the node socket; one local connection for each session

# On the computer of the operator:
export PODNET_RELAY_CONNECT_TOKEN=<connect token>
ssh -o ProxyCommand='podnet relay connect NAME' USER@NAME
podnet relay connect NAME --listen tcp://127.0.0.1:2222   # or a local port for each client

# On the host, at the end:
podnet relay stop NAME
```

* `podnet relay pair` asks the relay for a pair (`POST /v1/pair`). A pair lasts
  at most 72 h. The file is `relay/pair-NAME.json` in the state directory,
  with mode 0600. `--json` prints the name, the connect token and the end
  time. An old file `relay/NAME.json` is not read: make a new pair.
* `podnet relay node [NAME] --to TARGET` takes the pair with the most time left
  when no name is given. `TARGET` is `host:port` or `unix:/path`. The node
  answers each `open` with `ready` after its local connection is ready, or
  with `reject` and the cause. A lost node socket is opened again at once
  after a socket that served, else after a backoff with jitter (`pod-relay`
  of PodUtils/podcrates). The node warns 24 h, 6 h and 1 h before the pair
  expires. A node with no pair name takes the next stored pair at the
  expiry (a pair that `podnet relay pair` made since), with no new start. Its
  operators need the name and the connect token of the next pair. When the
  relay ends the pair (it expired with no next pair, or `podnet relay stop`
  ran), or refuses the node token (a 401 or 403 at the upgrade of the node
  socket), the node exits 78 and is not started again. A Close 1008 that
  names the token does not stop the node: it opens the socket again. When
  another node holds the name for 30 s, the node exits 69.
* `podnet relay connect NAME` waits for `ready`, then copies stdin and stdout.
  A name that is not a valid pair name exits 64.
  A refused session exits 69 with the cause from the node. A refused token
  exits 78. After the end of stdin, the session ends when the node closes,
  or 15 s (the idle time of the relay) after the last data. A close of the
  relay other than 1000 (for example 1009 at its byte limit) or a lost link
  exits 69, also after the end of stdin: the output can be cut.
* The relay authenticates tokens, not persons. Give the connect token only
  over a channel that you trust. Check the host key of SSH as usual.
* The relay sets its own limits; podnet does not enforce them. Measured on
  `tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev`: 64 MiB and 12 h for each session, and it can end
  a session after 180 s with no payload. Open a new session after a limit.

## Hosts and limits

* A list in `--relay` (comma-separated) is a preference of order. A host that
  fails with an error that another host can repair, or that says nothing while
  a host after it opens, is tried last for 10 minutes. A host that opens is
  tried first for the same time. One failure moves a host. No host is left
  out. The record is a private file in the state directory
  (`pod-relay` of PodUtils/podcrates).
* The budget of a stream through the relay (the edge leg of a tunnel and the
  MASQUE leg of WARP) follows the `limits` of the pool document of the relay
  (`max_session_bytes`, `max_session_ms`): 4 MiB under the byte cap and 30
  minutes under the time cap, never more than 60 MiB and 11.5 h. A relay with
  no `limits` keeps these values. The HTTP/2 edge leg still counts the
  constants (T-163).
* A pair is made on the control host of the relay only. The node and the
  operator use the first host of the list (T-200).

## Other uses of the relay

* `podnet serve --ingress relay --pair NAME` and `podnet git serve --ingress relay --pair NAME` put the
  file server and the git SSH server on the node of a pair ([serve.md](serve.md)).
* `podnet expose TARGET --via relay` starts a node for a local service ([forward.md](forward.md)).
* `--egress relay` (or `--transport relay`) sends the edge connection of a tunnel in a WebSocket to the
  relay ([tunnels.md](tunnels.md), "Edge protocol and transport"). `--egress relay` is also a network of
  `podnet forward` and of a router ([egress.md](egress.md)).
* `podnet warp nc --via-relay HOST PORT` and the relay path of the MASQUE connection ([warp.md](warp.md))
  use the same relay.
* `podnet relay connect` and `podnet relay node` take `--detach` ([background.md](background.md)).
* A program that uses the library gives a node a handler in place of a target:
  `relay_reverse::channel(depth)` returns a handler and a receiver. Each
  session that the relay opens is one end of a pipe; the receiver gives the
  other end with the session id. `relay_reverse::run_node_with` runs the node
  over the handler. No socket file is made, and a closed receiver refuses a
  session.
* `podnet doctor` tests the TCP and TLS path to the relay ([doctor.md](doctor.md)).

## SSH forward relay: `podnet ssh-relay`

Some hosted relays give a public URL for a unix socket through an SSH remote forward on port 443 (the
server prints the URL in its banner). `podnet ssh-relay` is the client for them. It publishes a unix
socket and keeps the session: when the relay ends the session, podnet connects again with a backoff and
prints the new URL.

```sh
podnet ssh-relay --socket /run/user/1000/origin.sock --detach
podnet ssh-relay --service serveo --socket /run/user/1000/origin.sock --detach
podnet ssh-relay --server relay.example.net:443 --user podnet \
  --url-skip dashboard.example.net --socket /run/user/1000/origin.sock --detach
```

* `--service NAME` selects a known relay. Its endpoints, its SSH user and its URL rule are data of
  `pod-services` (`pod_services::forward`). The default is `pinggy`. An unknown name exits 64 and lists the
  known relays. podnet holds no relay host.
* `--server HOST:PORT` replaces the endpoints of the relay. Use a port that the egress allows (443 for most
  proxies). With `--server` and no `--service`, the relay is not a known one: give `--user` and a URL rule
  (else exit 64). Without `--server`, podnet tries the plain SSH endpoints of the relay in order, and goes
  to the next endpoint on a transport error only.
* `--user USER` replaces the SSH user of the facts. podnet tries the methods in this order: a key made for
  the run (kept in memory only), no key (this also reads the list of methods of the relay), and an empty
  answer to keyboard-interactive (up to four rounds), when the relay offers it. It stops at the first
  success. It sends no password. When the relay takes none, the error names the methods that the relay
  offers. podnet checks RSA host keys (the relay Pinggy presents one) and keeps no known-hosts file.
* The banner of the relay can hold more than one URL, and a URL can cross two data frames. podnet reads the
  whole banner, then picks the URL. `--url-match TEXT` selects the tunnel URL: it holds this text (the
  tunnel domain of the relay). `--url-skip TEXT` removes a URL: it holds this text. Both are repeatable,
  and each replaces its list of the facts. The default skip list holds the dashboards of all known relays.
* `--remote-port PORT` (1 to 65535) is the port that the relay opens for the forward. Without it, podnet
  asks for port 0 and the relay chooses. A relay can refuse port 0 (the Sandhole demo needs 80). The
  service data has no such fact (T-319), so give the flag for such a relay. `--json` and the ready document
  show the port of the forward.
* `--socket PATH` is the unix socket of the origin. The relay opens one channel for each visitor, and
  podnet connects it to this socket. The origin must listen on the socket before the first visitor comes.
  The default is `origin.sock` in the private run directory of this user.
* `--connect-proxy HOST:PORT` reaches the relay through an HTTP CONNECT proxy. The default is a direct
  connection. `--proxy`, `--egress` and `--resolve` apply as for the other commands ([proxies.md](proxies.md)).
* `--json` prints each URL as one JSON line: `{"event": "ready" or "reconnected", "url", "remote_port",
  "relay"}`.
* `--detach`, `--name` and the other options of [background.md](background.md) work. The ready document
  has the URL. `podnet ps` shows the new URL after each reconnect.
* `podnet doctor --ssh-relay HOST:PORT --ssh-user USER [--connect-proxy HOST:PORT]` tests the relay with no
  session: the TCP connect (through the proxy of the process, or the given HTTP CONNECT proxy), the SSH banner
  and the login of the user. With no flag, it reads the relay of a running
  `ssh-relay` instance ([doctor.md](doctor.md)).

<!-- document: docs/egress.md -->

# Networks and `--egress`

A network is a way to send a flow out of this host. podnet names each network with a spec: one text in
one form for each command. The same specs are used by `--egress`, `podnet forward --network`,
`podnet pod -x`, `podnet bench` and the `networks` of a router file ([router.md](router.md)).

## The registry

| Scheme | Forms of the spec | What it is | Carries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `direct` | `direct` | TCP and UDP from this host, with no proxy. | TCP, UDP |
| proxy | `http://[USER:PASS@]HOST[:PORT]`, `socks5://...`, `socks5h://...`, `SCHEME+unix:/PATH`, `SCHEME://unix:/PATH`, `SCHEME+exec:COMMAND`, `unix:/PATH`, `HOST:PORT` | An HTTP CONNECT proxy or a SOCKS5 proxy. | TCP |
| `relay` | `relay`, `relay:URL`, `relay:HOST` | The WebSocket relay (`PODNET_RELAY`, default `https://tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev`). IPv4 TCP only. | TCP |
| `tailscale` | `tailscale:/PATH/tailscaled.sock` | A tailnet, through the LocalAPI of `tailscaled` ([networks.md](networks.md)). | TCP |
| `netbird` | `netbird`, `netbird:[PORT]` | The SOCKS5 listener of NetBird in netstack mode on `127.0.0.1:PORT` (default 1080). The target must be an IP address ([networks.md](networks.md)). | TCP |
| `wg` | `wg:FILE` | A WireGuard peer of a wg-quick file, on a userspace stack. The target must be an IP address ([networks.md](networks.md)). | TCP, UDP |
| `peer` | `peer:FINGERPRINT/SERVICE` | One stream to a service of a peer, over a link that a running `podnet link connect` or `link listen` instance holds ([link.md](link.md)). A peer way: it meets a peer and dials no destination. | TCP |

* A spec with no scheme (`HOST:PORT`) is a SOCKS5 proxy, as in `podnet pod -x`.
* `socks5://` resolves the name on this host. `socks5h://` gives the name to the proxy.
* `SCHEME+exec:COMMAND` starts `COMMAND` with `sh -c` for each connection and uses its stdin and stdout
  as the proxy connection (see [proxies.md](proxies.md)).
* An error about a spec shows the spec without its user and password.
* `warp` is not a network of the registry. Use `podnet warp proxy` ([warp.md](warp.md)) or
  `tunnel --transport warp`.

## `--egress`

`--egress SPEC` is a flag of each command that opens connections. It selects the way out of the process,
and it replaces the older flags:

| `--egress` | Same as |
| --- | --- |
| `direct` | `--no-proxy` |
| A proxy URL | `--proxy URL` |
| `relay`, `relay:URL` | `--transport relay` and `--relay URL` |

* `--egress` beside `--proxy`, `--no-proxy`, `--transport` or `--relay` is a usage error (exit 64), because
  the two flags name one way.
* With `podnet pod`, each `--egress` is one hop `-x SPEC` of the chain, in its order. The forms
  `tailscale:/PATH`, `netbird:[PORT]` and `unix:/PATH` are hops of a pod. The relay is not a hop of a
  pod.
* `peer:FINGERPRINT/SERVICE` is a peer way. A consumer that dials a destination (`--egress`, `podnet forward --network`, `pod -x`)
  refuses it with exit 64. Use `podnet forward -L LISTEN=peer:FINGERPRINT/SERVICE` ([forward.md](forward.md)). A `PORT` after
  `peer:` (`peer:1080`) is still the SOCKS5 hop of a host named `peer`.
* `wg:FILE` is not a hop of a pod, and no process command takes it in `--egress`: each gives one line.
  Use `podnet forward --network wg:FILE` or a `networks:` entry of a router file.
* `tailscale:/PATH` is a hop of a pod and the only hop of its chain. A command that is not `pod` refuses
  `--egress tailscale:/PATH` with one line: use `podnet pod`, `podnet forward --network` or a router file.
* A spec that the command cannot use is a usage error with one line that names the spec.
* `podnet forward --network SPEC` selects the network of the forwards ([forward.md](forward.md)). Its default
  is the way out of the process.

```sh
podnet --egress socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8080
podnet --egress relay tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8080
podnet --egress direct doctor
podnet pod --egress socks5://proxy-a:1080 --egress tailscale:/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock -- ssh host
podnet bench --egress socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 https://example.com/
```

<!-- document: docs/proxies.md -->

# Proxies, DNS and TLS roots

This page gives how podnet reaches the network from a host with a proxy: the proxy URL forms, the order of
the proxy sources, the DNS chain and the TLS roots. `--egress` is the same choice as a network spec
([egress.md](egress.md)).

## Proxies and DNS

Each connection of podnet (the quick-tunnel API, DNS over HTTPS, the HTTP/2
edge leg, the WARP API, MASQUE, the fetch of the public URL) takes the same
proxy:

```sh
podnet --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:1080 tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8080
PODNET_PROXY="$PROXY_URL" podnet demo --exit-on-verify    # PROXY_URL: http://[USER:PASSWORD@]HOST:PORT
NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,.internal podnet warp register
podnet --no-proxy tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8080
```

* The order: `--proxy` (or `PODNET_PROXY`), then `HTTPS_PROXY`,
  `https_proxy`, `ALL_PROXY`, `all_proxy`. A variable that is empty or does
  not parse is skipped. `--no-proxy` uses none.
* Percent-encode `/ ? # @ :` in the user and the password of a proxy URL
  (for example `%2F` for `/`).
* `http://` uses `CONNECT`. `socks5://` resolves the name on this host;
  `socks5h://` gives the name to the proxy. podnet refuses `socks4://` and
  `https://`.
* A proxy on a unix socket: `socks5h+unix:/PATH` (also
  `socks5h://unix:/PATH`), or `http+unix:/PATH`.
* A proxy at the stdin and the stdout of a command, when the only way out
  is a byte channel (issue 129): `--proxy 'http+exec:ssh gw nc 127.0.0.1
  3128'`. Each connection starts the command once, with `sh -c`, as the
  `ProxyCommand` of SSH; its stderr is the stderr of podnet. Only `--proxy`
  and `PODNET_PROXY` take `+exec:`: a variable of another tool does not start
  a program. QUIC legs need UDP and do not use it.
* Without `--proxy` and `--no-proxy`, podnet reads `HTTPS_PROXY`,
  `https_proxy`, `ALL_PROXY` and `all_proxy`. `NO_PROXY` names the targets
  that do not use the proxy.
* When no proxy variable is set, podnet takes the proxy of the first tool
  config that names one: `~/.gitconfig` and `~/.config/git/config`
  (`http.proxy`), `~/.npmrc` (`https-proxy`, else `proxy`),
  `~/.config/pip/pip.conf` and `~/.pip/pip.conf` (`proxy`),
  `/etc/gitconfig`, `/etc/pip.conf`, and `/etc/environment`. The log names
  the file. `--no-proxy` turns it off.
* With a proxy, `--protocol auto` does not try QUIC on UDP 7844 (no proxy
  carries UDP), and podnet prints one line that says so. `--protocol quic`
  keeps QUIC, with a warning.
* With a user and a password, podnet sends Basic. A proxy that answers 407
  with a Digest challenge (RFC 7616: MD5, MD5-sess, SHA-256,
  SHA-256-sess, `qop=auth`) gets the Digest answer on a new connection.
  Another 407 gets a message with the schemes that the proxy asks for. No
  NTLM.

A direct connection resolves the name with this chain: a pin of
`--resolve HOST=IP` or `PODNET_RESOLVE`, the system resolver, then DNS over
HTTPS by IP address at Cloudflare (1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1) and Google (8.8.8.8,
8.8.4.4). It tries each address of the name, and starts the next attempt
250 ms after the one before.

## TLS roots

podnet checks the certificate of each TLS server that it connects to. Behind a
proxy that inspects TLS, give the root of the proxy:

```sh
SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/corp-root.pem podnet tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8080
podnet --ca-file /etc/corp-root.pem warp register
```

`--ca-file` and `SSL_CERT_FILE` replace the other roots. Without them, podnet
trusts `podnet-ca.pem` beside the binary, the first system bundle that it can
read (for example `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`), and the Mozilla
roots compiled into podnet. `podnet status` shows the roots in `tls_roots`. See
`SECURITY.md`.

## Front doors

A front door is a listener that speaks SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT. The listener detects the protocol from the
first byte. These commands run the same door (`crates/podnet-netns/src/door.rs`, T-061):

| Command | The way of a flow |
| --- | --- |
| `podnet pod --serve LISTEN -x UPSTREAM` | The chain of `-x`, or the chain that a `-r` rule chooses. |
| `podnet net proxy` | The virtual network of the stack of the command (`--map`, `--forward`, `--switch`). |
| `podnet net tailscale` | `tailscaled`, through its LocalAPI. |
| `podnet route` | A network or a group of the router ([router.md](router.md)). |

`podnet warp proxy` has its own door until the take of `pod-warp` (T-050).

The door has these rules for each client:

* The client has 30 s to send its first byte and its request. A client that is too slow gets SOCKS5 `0x04`
  or HTTP 504, and the door closes the connection.
* The door serves 1024 live clients at one time. It closes a client that comes over the cap.
* The door waits at most 30 s for the connection to the far end. `net tailscale` waits 10 s and `net proxy`
  waits 5 s.
* The failure of a dial gives the reply by its class: a refusal of a rule or of a policy is SOCKS5 `0x02` and
  HTTP 403; a time limit is SOCKS5 `0x04` and HTTP 504; any other failure is a general failure (or a
  host unreachable, when the text says refused or denied) and HTTP 502. An HTTP answer has a short text
  body.
* A request with port 0 takes the port of `--port` (`net proxy` and `net tailscale`).
* `pod --serve`, `net proxy` and `net tailscale` take SOCKS5 and CONNECT only. A plain `http://` request
  gets 405. `net proxy` and `net tailscale` end a flow after 300 s.
* BIND gets SOCKS5 `0x07` (command not supported). UDP ASSOCIATE goes through the first upstream for
  `pod --serve`, and gets `0x07` for `net proxy` and `net tailscale`.

### Early reply

`podnet pod --serve LISTEN -x UPSTREAM --early-reply` answers a client before the dial. It is off by
default. Use it on an upstream of high latency (a satellite or a cellular link), where the time to the first
byte of a new connection is three round trips: the TCP connect, the method reply and the reply of the
request.

With the option, the door does this for a SOCKS5 CONNECT and an HTTP CONNECT:

1. The door checks the target against the rules of `-r`. A target that a rule refuses gets its real answer
   (SOCKS5 `0x02`, HTTP 403) with no early reply.
2. The door answers success (SOCKS5 `0x00` with the bound address `0.0.0.0:0`, HTTP 200). The client sends
   its first bytes at once.
3. The door dials and holds the bytes of the client in the meantime. It holds at most 64 KiB. When the hold
   is full, the door stops to read, and the TCP window of the client closes. A client that ends its side
   before the dial is done has its end sent to the upstream after the held bytes.
4. For a SOCKS5 upstream without a user, the door sends the greeting and the request in one write. For
   the last hop, it writes the held bytes behind the request and reads the two replies later. A hop in
   front of the last hop sends the greeting and the request in one write and reads both replies. A hop with
   a user and a password runs the serial handshake, because the method reply must come before the next bytes.
   An HTTP upstream runs its serial handshake. The door still answers the client early, and holds the
   bytes of the client until the upstream says yes.
5. The wait for the replies has the same 30 s limit as the dial.

What the client sees when the flow fails after the early reply:

| The failure | Without the option | With the option |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The upstream refuses (a reply code other than `0x00`) | SOCKS5 `0x01` and HTTP 502 | The client has the success reply. The connection then closes with no byte. |
